highlights.text: Withdrawing from a thing and parting from it (التباعد والمزايلة)
Creating (الخلق)
الْبَارِئُ (the Creator/Fashioner) is God
الْبُرْء = soundness from sickness
Declaring oneself quit / disowning
The poet Umayya pairs the term with al-Khāliq and al-Muṣawwir
highlights.note: Umayya, named in the entry (pre-Islamic era)

highlights.text: whiteness (bayāḍ), the opposite of blackness
adjective abyaḍ (white)
Verb: ibyaḍḍa / yabyaḍḍu (to turn white)
bayḍ (eggs), sing. bayḍa — named for its whiteness
because whiteness was regarded as the finest of colours
is white of Quḍāʿa
one core idea: submission/compliance (inqiyād) and lowliness or abasement (dhull)
Al-dīn is "obedience."
under the king's ṭāʿa (authority/obedience)
To deal on credit (giving or taking) is dāyana
Shāhid (from Imruʾ al-Qays): "like your wont (ka-dīnika)
Debt is humiliation by day and grief by night.
one core sense — cutting a thing (qaṭʿ)
To fabricate: فَرَى كَذِبًا (farā kadhiban) = to invent/concoct a lie
الْفَرَى also = the marvellous/astonishing thing (same as al-fariyy)
A cited line uses تَفْرِينَ الْفَرِيّ for someone who "spoke much about a thing and magnified it."
a single sound root meaning a thing passing into or through something else and becoming fixed there
Resentment that works its way into the breast.
In the case of booty, ghulūl means hiding an item so it is not returned for division
He cites al-Namir, who prays that God repay Jamra, daughter of Nawfal, "as one who betrays a trust (mughill) and lies" is repaid.
In the Prophet's saying "no ighlāl and no islāl," ighlāl is treachery
"covering / concealing," combined with a sense of intensity or hardship.
Al-ghamra — total absorption in falsehood and idle amusement
ghamarātu l-mawt, "the death-throes/agonies,"
Illustrated with a line from the poet Kuthayyir describing such a man's smile.
one sound root whose core idea is intensity and strength
الْكَرْب (al-karb) — intense grief
Shāhid — al-Ḥuṭayʾa: a people who, when they make a bond for their neighbour, fasten the bucket-strap and then fasten the karab-knot above it
they all trace back to one core sense: ease, pleasant living, and wellbeing
a benefit God bestows on His servant, such as wealth and livelihood
luxuriating and pleasant living, cited from Q 44:27 (al-Dukhān)
By the same logic الأنعام (anʿām) means livestock/beasts.
the verb of praise, opposite of بِئْسَ (biʾsa, dispraise)
from two sound roots that lie close together: (1) a thing's falling short of its full extent, and (2) confinement or restraint.
Transitive: qaṣṣara — "I shortened the garment or the rope."
qaṣartuhu = "I confined/imprisoned him"; maqṣūr = confined
qāṣirat al-ṭarf = a woman who restrains her gaze
a sound root (aṣl ṣaḥīḥ) meaning "cutting a thing quickly, crosswise"
Al-qiṭṭ is said to be the written deed (ṣakk) for a gift (jāʾiza).
Al-Aʿshā uses the plural, quṭūṭ, in a line on King al-Nuʿmān "giving out the quṭūṭ" on the day the poet met him.
those who said it meant, as it were, the documents of reward they are given in the Hereafter
one family built on the number "four" and its derivatives
أربعة (four), أربعون (forty), رُبع (a quarter), رُباع (four at a time)
a single root whose core idea is throwing, pelting, or flinging
الرَّدَى is destruction; رَدِيَ يَرْدَى = "he perished"; أَرْدَاهُ اللَّهُ = "God destroyed him."
التَّرَدِّي is plunging into a chasm
one single, regular meaning: assisting and backing someone by giving — a gift or other support
الرَّفْد (al-rafd) is the verbal noun of "rafadahu" — he gave him [something]
"Urfidtu al-māl" — I was given/granted the wealth
Ibn Fāris cites a line of al-Farazdaq mentioning "Iraq and its two Rāfids."
A ḥadīth uses it: "the fayʾ [war-gained wealth] becomes rifd"
one central image — the leg/foot (rijl) of any creature that has one
الرِّجْل (al-rijl) — the leg/foot of a human or animal
foot-soldiers/infantry (al-rajjāla), so named because they travel on their feet
الرَّجُل (al-rajul) — a "man," a single adult male
Cited verse: a vow to visit "the House of God, on foot and barefoot."
**flinging or casting a thing away**
رَمَيْتُ الشَّيْءَ أَرْمِيهِ — "I threw (or shot at) the thing, I throw it."
"going in search of something" — a compound notion combining *going* and *seeking*.
Al-sa'āma is weariness/tedium that comes from something continuing too long
Supporting verse of poetry: "I have grown weary of life's burdens; whoever lives eighty years grows weary"
the succession of many things, each connected to the next
glossed as ensuring the proportion between rivet and hole is exact, neither too tight nor too loose
al-sard — a collective term for chainmail and similar ring-linked work
وَرى (with fatḥa; also the dialectal wariya with kasra) = to produce/give out fire
وارَيْتُ الشيءَ = I hid the thing; تَوارى = he hid himself
وَراءَ (warāʾ) = "behind," but can also mean "in front / ahead,"
Al-Jawharī reads the Qurʾānic "and behind them was a king" (18:79) as meaning "ahead of them."
a single governing sense, which he takes from al-Khalīl: **concealing something**
خَدَعْتُ الرجل — "I deceived the man," glossed as ختلته (I tricked / caught him off guard)
Cited proverb: «الحرب خُدَعة» ("war is trickery")
"to increase, grow, add, exceed"
Of a thing growing of itself: زاد ("increased") — of water or wealth
Of causing growth: God "increased him in wealth"
Of exceeding: "he exceeded what he intended"
Cited from Dhū al-Iṣbaʿ al-ʿAdwānī: "you are a company exceeding a hundred; so gather your whole affair and scheme against me"
